en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-Attadaṇḍa-sūtra*, translated by an unknown person;
now appended to the Catalogue of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Vairaṭya at a place where there were many trees. With...
Accompanied by a community of monks— five hundred bhikṣus—
in the fullness of the fifteenth day of the month, at midnight when all was still and tranquil, the assembly of bhikṣus questioned one another.
At that time, the deva Candanadūṣī, assuming a celestial form and radiating divine majesty and brilliance, came forward directly toward the Buddha.

Having arrived before the Buddha, he removed all the precious jewels from his body and set them aside, then donned a single robe. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet; having completed his salutation, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Among the disciples of the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past Buddhas, there was a sutra titled the *Aṭṭhaka*; the disciples of the present Buddha now likewise recite this *Aṭṭhaka Sūtra*.”
"I pray that the Buddha will preach this sutra for me, so that his disciples may receive and uphold it.
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
Candanadatta bowed his head to the ground and withdrew to sit at one side.
The Buddha then spoke this sutra for the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"I have preached the *Aṭṭhaka-vagga* for you; listen well and take it to heart, reflecting upon it so that you do not forget it."
The bhikṣu said, “I pray that the Buddha will speak; I shall receive all the sūtras and precepts.
The Buddha said:
"There are eight matters regarding giving. What are these eight?
A foolish person gives a gift, yet they do not understand where its merit and goodness reside."
Having practiced giving, one realizes that the world is not permanent, yet the deluded person maintains it to be permanent.
Suffering in the world is boundless, yet the foolish person maintains it to be pleasure.
Regarding all that exists in the world, the foolish person says, "This is mine; it can be obtained permanently."
The people of the world are all deluded; regarding that which is impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome, the foolish take it to be good.

They do not know that by doing good one obtains good, and by doing evil one obtains evil. When a fool gives to others, he does not discern the depth of their virtue. Yet, if one maintains a virtuous mind in giving to those who have attained the Way, the merit is immeasurable.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"By what means is it known that fools do not understand giving?
There are ten causes and conditions."
What are these ten? The foolish person, when practicing giving, does not know that it is what is honored; they believe that it is the giver themselves who obtains the merit.
The foolish person does not give to others with a sincere heart.
When a fool gives to others, he does not do so with reverence at the time of giving;
he does not give with his own hands, but instructs another to give, and when giving to others, he does not desire their merit.
If he does not immediately obtain that merit, he forgets it because of his own self-centeredness.
When a fool gives to a Buddha, a Pratyekabuddha, or an Arhat, he cannot know for himself that his merit is great;
when a fool gives, he does not believe in the Buddha, the Pratyekabuddha, the Arhat, the Anāgāmin, the Sakṛdāgāmin, or the Srotāpanna,
regarding all such acts as wasted and useless, with no existence in future lives.
"The fool gives because he desires only a name, wishing for others to praise him.
This is called the giving of a fool.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Candanadatta and the bhikṣus were all filled with joy; they came forward and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra on Aṭaḥ and Bahudhātuka Spoken by the Buddha.
